network.overall_strategy: This evidence-weighted network treats pyruvic acid as the main proximal hub because pyruvate-to-alanine chemistry is the best supported experimental node, while also retaining direct aldehyde/cyanide and HCN-free surface routes on equal footing. Ten pathways are generated by combining two hydrothermal pyruvate-source modules with four pyruvate-to-alanine modules, plus two direct surface routes. All experimentally grounded routes converge on an alanine pool that is expected to be racemic; a final late enantioenrichment node is included explicitly and marked speculative because no robust prebiotic route to selectively make L-alanine is known.

reactions.name: Hydrothermal CO2/H2 fixation to pyruvic acid

conditions.other: alkaline H2-rich vent fluid; pyruvate expected only at low concentration

reactions.mechanism: Mineral-assisted reduction of CO2-derived C1 species followed by C-C coupling to a C3 alpha-keto acid.
reactions.reasoning: Pyruvate formation from CO2 and H2 on greigite, magnetite, and awaruite is experimentally supported in alkaline hydrothermal systems, making pyruvic acid a plausible hydrothermal hub even though reported concentrations are only micromolar and concentration remains unresolved (Preiner et al., 2020). This node is therefore included as a low-flux but chemically grounded entry to keto-acid chemistry.

reactions.name: NiS-mediated acetylene/CO carbonylation to pyruvic acid

conditions.other: subseafloor carbonylation/hydration chemistry; short residence times favored because pyruvate is thermally labile

reactions.mechanism: NiS-promoted acetyleno/carboxydotrophic carbonylation and hydration sequence yielding the C3 alpha-keto acid as a net product.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and co-workers reported pyruvate formation from acetylene and CO on NiS above 100 degrees C, providing a distinct hydrothermal C3 entry that does not rely on direct bulk CO2 fixation (Huber et al., 2020). The step is written as a net transformation to keep the network compact; the main critique is that pyruvate is thermally fragile, so residence time at elevated temperature must remain limited (Miller and Bada, 1988).

reactions.name: Green-rust reductive amination of pyruvic acid

conditions.other: pH about 10; Fe(II):Fe(III) about 1:1; NH3-rich; lower pH favors lactate instead

reactions.mechanism: Pyruvic acid first forms an imine/iminopyruvate with ammonia, then receives a two-electron reduction to the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Mixed-valence iron oxyhydroxides are among the strongest mild hydrothermal systems for alanine formation from pyruvate, with best alanine selectivity near Fe(II):Fe(III)=1:1 and pH 10, while pH 7 strongly suppresses alanine and favors lactate (Barge et al., 2019). The reaction is written with H2 as the net electron equivalent so the redox balance is explicit, although experimentally the reducing power is carried largely by the mineral redox state itself.

reactions.name: Electroreduced FeS reductive amination of pyruvic acid

conditions.other: pH 9.6; about 0.5 M NH3; vent-like negative potential required to pre-reduce the mineral

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with pyruvic acid to an imine equivalent that is reduced on a strongly reducing FeS-derived surface.
reactions.reasoning: Electroreduced FeS generated under vent-like negative potentials aminates pyruvate very efficiently under alkaline conditions, with near-complete conversion reported in favorable runs (Kitadai et al., 2019). Here H2 represents the net reducing equivalent supplied by the pre-reduced FeS/Fe0 surface; the geochemical challenge is sustaining both the reducing potential and NH3-rich conditions in natural systems.

reactions.name: Native nickel/H2 reductive amination of pyruvic acid

conditions.other: pH 7-8; NH3 can be millimolar to tens of millimolar; lower NH3 still gives measurable alanine

reactions.mechanism: Ni0 activates H2 and reduces the imine/iminopyruvate formed from pyruvic acid and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Native nickel under H2 gives one of the most geochemically attractive catalytic pyruvate-to-alanine systems because it works at mild temperature and with substantially less NH3 than older Fe-mineral work, while still giving significant alanine yields (Kaur et al., 2024). Its main weaknesses are the need for available Ni0 and sustained H2 pressure.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin formation from pyruvic acid

conditions.other: cyanide/ammonia solution; dissolved CO2/HCO3- required mechanistically although not net consumed

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the alpha-keto acid framework, followed by carbamylation/cyclization to the hydantoin.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti and co-workers showed that alpha-keto acids enter Bucherer-Bergs chemistry under prebiotically relevant aqueous conditions, and that dissolved CO2/HCO3- is mechanistically essential even when it is not net consumed (Pulletikurti et al., 2022). This is an important bridge between metabolic carbon skeletons and cyanide chemistry, but it inherits the unresolved requirement that pyruvate and cyanide must be co-localized.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic ring opening of 5-methylhydantoin

conditions.other: mild hydrolytic ring opening in aqueous solution

reactions.mechanism: Water opens the hydantoin ring to the corresponding N-carbamoyl amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Ring opening of hydantoins to N-carbamoyl amino acids is the expected next stage of Bucherer-Bergs chemistry and is chemically more realistic than collapsing the whole route into a single pyruvate-to-alanine step (Pulletikurti et al., 2022). Including this intermediate preserves mechanistic continuity and stoichiometric correctness.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis and decarbamylation of N-carbamoylalanine

conditions.other: continued aqueous processing to release alanine

reactions.mechanism: Further hydrolysis cleaves the carbamoyl group, releasing alanine along with CO2 and NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Once the N-carbamoyl intermediate is formed, its hydrolysis closes the Bucherer-Bergs branch cleanly to alanine without requiring an unsupported catalyst (Pulletikurti et al., 2022). This step also makes explicit the release of CO2 and NH3 that is hidden in overcompressed one-step encodings.

reactions.name: Strecker aminonitrile formation from acetaldehyde

conditions.other: HCN-rich aqueous pool; adequate NH3 suppresses diversion toward cyanohydrin chemistry

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde forms an imine with ammonia, and cyanide capture gives the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the classical Strecker entry to alanine. Miller-type discharge chemistry and later cyanosulfidic networks both supply compatible HCN and aldehyde feedstocks, while isotopic work supports Strecker chemistry as a real source of alanine in natural samples (Miller, 1953; Cleaves et al., 2008; Patel et al., 2015; Chimiak et al., 2022).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alpha-aminopropionitrile to alanine

conditions.other: prolonged hydration during acidic/basic cycling or wet-dry reworking

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile is hydrated through amide-like intermediates to the carboxylic acid, releasing ammonia overall.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of the aminonitrile is the second canonical Strecker stage and should be represented explicitly because water is chemically required for conversion to alanine (Miller, 1953; Chimiak et al., 2022). This separation avoids hiding nitrile hydrolysis inside an overpacked one-step Strecker node.

reactions.name: Thiol-catalyzed triose route from glyceraldehyde to alanine
reactions.mechanism: Thiol-assisted dehydration of glyceraldehyde to methylglyoxal-like intermediates is followed by imine/hemithioacetal chemistry and hydrolysis to alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Weber demonstrated that glyceraldehyde plus ammonia can yield alanine in water and that a thiol catalyst accelerates the chemistry markedly, making this a distinct HCN-free surface route (Weber, 1985; Weber, 1998). The drawbacks are low yield, long timescale, and the unresolved prebiotic source of the thiol catalyst.

reactions.name: Speculative enantioenrichment of alanine pool to L-alanine

conditions.other: dry-film or ice-residue UV irradiation followed by wet-dry recrystallization; only small ee is demonstrated experimentally

reactions.mechanism: Weak enantioselective photolysis or differential survival seeds a small L excess that is then assumed to undergo physical amplification during repeated cycling.
reactions.reasoning: No experimentally supported prebiotic route makes L-alanine directly. CPL photolysis can induce only percent-level enantiomeric excesses in alanine or its precursors, and natural claims of substantial extraterrestrial L-alanine excess are disputed; later Murchison and Bennu measurements are racemic (Meinert et al., 2014; Modica et al., 2014; Pizzarello and Cronin, 1998; Glavin et al., 2021; Glavin, Dworkin et al., 2025). This node is therefore explicitly speculative and is included only because the requested target is L-alanine rather than racemic alanine.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation plus green-rust amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal CO2/H2 fixation supplies pyruvic acid, which is aminated on green rust before a late speculative surface enrichment step.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation plus electroreduced FeS amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal CO2/H2 fixation supplies pyruvic acid, which is aminated on electroreduced FeS/Fe0 and then passed to the late enrichment module.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation plus native Ni/H2 amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal CO2/H2 fixation supplies pyruvic acid, which is aminated on native nickel under H2 before speculative L-selection.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation plus Bucherer-Bergs bridge
pathways.description: Hydrothermal pyruvic acid is handed off to cyanide-rich surface chemistry, where Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin chemistry yields alanine before late enrichment; co-localization of pyruvate and cyanide is the open problem.

pathways.name: Acetylene/CO route plus green-rust amination
pathways.description: NiS-mediated hydrothermal carbonylation of acetylene and CO forms pyruvic acid, followed by green-rust amination and late enrichment.

pathways.name: Acetylene/CO route plus electroreduced FeS amination
pathways.description: NiS-mediated hydrothermal pyruvic acid formation is coupled to electroreduced FeS amination, then to the speculative L-selection module.

pathways.name: Acetylene/CO route plus native Ni/H2 amination
pathways.description: A hydrothermal acetyleno/carboxydotrophic pyruvic acid source is combined with native Ni/H2 amination before late enrichment.

pathways.name: Acetylene/CO route plus Bucherer-Bergs bridge
pathways.description: Hydrothermal pyruvic acid from acetylene/CO chemistry is bridged into cyanide-bearing surface pools through Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin chemistry, then sent to late enrichment.

pathways.name: Direct surface Strecker route
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde, HCN, and ammonia form alpha-aminopropionitrile, which hydrolyzes to alanine before the late speculative enrichment step.

pathways.name: Direct thiol-assisted triose route
pathways.description: Glyceraldehyde and ammonia react in a thiol-catalyzed surface route to alanine, followed by the explicit but weakly supported L-enrichment module.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Coherent hydrothermal route to a racemic alanine pool, but rxn_001 is only a low-yield net module unless specific mineral catalysts and concentrating effects are stated. The green-rust amination is literature-grounded, yet the node as written uses H2 rather than the mixed-valence mineral redox chemistry actually shown, and the final L-enrichment step is unsupported.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_001 with explicit stoichiometry: 3 CO2 + 5 H2 -> pyruvic acid + 3 H2O, and specify the hydrothermal mineral system and expected low pyruvate yield.
Specify green-rust conditions for rxn_003: mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III), alkaline pH, high NH3, and lactate competition; do not treat H2 as the sole reductant for this literature node.
Add an explicit transfer or concentration step before any surface enrichment, or retarget the pathway to racemic alanine if strict evidence is required.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This branch improves on P1 because electroreduced FeS amination is experimentally strong, but it needs a sustained negative potential, alkaline conditions, and high NH3. rxn_001 remains under-specified and low-yield, and the final surface enrichment to L-alanine is not demonstrated.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_001 as 3 CO2 + 5 H2 -> pyruvic acid + 3 H2O and specify the mineral catalysts and concentration constraints.
Specify the electrochemical setting for rxn_004, including sustained negative potential, alkaline pH, and NH3 loading.
Add an explicit hydrothermal-to-surface transfer or concentration step before rxn_012, or stop at racemic alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Among the stronger pyruvate branches because Ni/H2 reductive amination is directly supported in the literature, but the pyruvate source remains the bottleneck and the Ni/H2 conditions need to be explicit. Final conversion to L-alanine remains speculative.
suggestions: Correct rxn_001 to 3 CO2 + 5 H2 -> pyruvic acid + 3 H2O and specify a realistic mineral-mediated hydrothermal source plus concentration mechanism.
Specify native Ni or Ni-bearing metal, H2 pressure, pH, and NH3 loading for rxn_005.
Either justify transport to a surface enrichment setting or retarget the product as racemic alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin and N-carbamoylalanine intermediates make this branch mechanistically coherent, but rxn_006 should explicitly include CO2 or HCO3- as essential for Bucherer-Bergs chemistry. The pathway also needs a justified transfer of pyruvate from hydrothermal generation to surface cyanide chemistry, and the last L-enrichment node is unsupported.
suggestions: Correct rxn_001 stoichiometry and specify a realistic mineral-mediated pyruvate source.
Amend rxn_006 to include explicit CO2 or HCO3- or carbonate, since Bucherer-Bergs chemistry is not well represented without it.
Add a justified hydrothermal-to-surface transport or concentration step and treat rxn_012 only as speculative enrichment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Acetylene and CO carbonylation gives a better specified pyruvate-source module than direct CO2 and H2 fixation, but NiS and hydrothermal conditions must be explicit. Green-rust amination still needs mixed-valence iron chemistry rather than direct H2, and the L step is speculative.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_002 as C2H2 + CO + 2 H2O -> pyruvic acid + H2 and specify NiS-mediated hydrothermal conditions.
Specify mixed-valence green rust, alkaline pH, NH3 concentration, and lactate competition for rxn_003.
Add a transfer or concentration step before surface enrichment, or stop at racemic alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: One of the better hydrothermal branches: the acetylene and CO to pyruvate module has experimental precedent and electroreduced FeS amination is strong. Remaining weaknesses are the missing NiS, temperature, and electrochemical details, no explicit transport to the surface enrichment step, and no credible L-selective chemistry.
suggestions: Correct rxn_002 stoichiometry and add explicit NiS and hydrothermal temperature or pressure details.
Specify the electrochemical setting for rxn_004: sustained negative potential, alkaline pH, and NH3 concentration.
Replace or weaken rxn_012 unless a concrete enrichment mechanism is provided.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strongest pyruvate-based branch in the network. Ni/H2 amination of pyruvate is well supported, and the acetylene and CO source is experimentally precedented. Still, rxn_002 should be written with 2 H2O and explicit NiS high-temperature conditions, and rxn_012 does not genuinely solve the L-alanine problem.
suggestions: Correct rxn_002 to C2H2 + CO + 2 H2O -> pyruvic acid + H2 and add explicit NiS or related sulfide conditions.
Specify native Ni or Ni-bearing metal, H2 pressure, pH, and NH3 loading for rxn_005.
Either justify transport to a surface enrichment setting or retarget the product as racemic alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Mechanistically coherent bridge from pyruvate to alanine via hydantoin, but the upstream pyruvate module still needs explicit NiS hydrothermal conditions and rxn_006 needs CO2 or HCO3- to match the literature. Cross-environment transfer and the unsupported L-enrichment step remain the main weaknesses.
suggestions: Correct rxn_002 stoichiometry and specify NiS-mediated hydrothermal carbonylation conditions.
Amend rxn_006 to include CO2 or HCO3- explicitly and describe the Bucherer-Bergs aqueous conditions.
Add a transport or concentration step from hydrothermal pyruvate production to surface cyanide chemistry, and keep rxn_012 clearly speculative.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Best-supported branch to racemic alanine. Strecker formation from acetaldehyde, NH3, and HCN is classic and prebiotically relevant, and nitrile hydrolysis to alanine is plausible. The fixable issue is rxn_010 stoichiometry, which should consume 2 H2O, while the decisive remaining problem is that rxn_012 lacks a robust prebiotic basis for making L-alanine.
suggestions: Correct rxn_010 stoichiometry to alpha-aminopropionitrile + 2 H2O -> alanine + NH3.
Specify hydrolysis conditions and note the cyanohydrin or lactate side-path issue when NH3 is low.
If the target must remain L-alanine, replace rxn_012 with a concrete small-ee enrichment mechanism and treat it only as enrichment, not full selective synthesis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A real literature route exists, but only as a low-yield, slow, thiol-dependent surface chemistry. As written, the key thiol catalyst is omitted, so the net step is too compressed, and even the supported route only gives small racemic alanine yields. The L-enrichment node is again unsupported.
suggestions: Add the required thiol catalyst explicitly and justify its prebiotic availability.
Specify the long reaction time and pH and temperature window from the Weber experiments; do not present rxn_011 as a simple high-yield step.
Retarget racemic alanine or provide a concrete enrichment mechanism instead of the unsupported rxn_012.

evaluation.network_feedback: Structurally this is a valid, connected network with sufficient node count and no RDKit-unbalanced reactions. It aligns well with the literature by covering the major experimentally supported racemic-alanine families and by explicitly flagging chirality as unresolved. The strongest individual branch is P9, and among pyruvate-based branches P7 is the best supported. Main weaknesses are under-specified hydrothermal source modules, omission of explicit mineral or electrochemical conditions and lactate competition in pyruvate aminations, missing essential CO2 or HCO3- in rxn_006, missing thiol catalysis in rxn_011, and unmodeled transport or concentration for hydrothermal-to-surface handoffs. Correct rxn_001 to 3 CO2 + 5 H2 -> pyruvic acid + 3 H2O, rxn_002 to C2H2 + CO + 2 H2O -> pyruvic acid + H2, and rxn_010 to alpha-aminopropionitrile + 2 H2O -> alanine + NH3. In its current form the network credibly reaches racemic alanine pools, but it does not yet convincingly achieve L-alanine because rxn_012 is speculative and no robust prebiotic L-selective route is known.
